rv.q: Your eyes are pretty much guaranteed to start stinging before the first act is over, and by the play’s end even people who think they have no patience for polemical theater may find their resistance has melted into tears.
This is tough, unflinching drama staged and performed by people with a fierce emotional investment in telling this story and keeping this painful history alive for generations inclined to forget.

It’s true that "The Normal Heart," Larry Kramer’s fiery 1985 docu-like drama about the AIDS pandemic, suffers from agit-prop agita, even in this first-rate production starring Joe Mantello and Ellen Barkin and co-helmed with enormous heart by Joel Grey and George C. Wolfe.

Larry Kramer's furious 1985 drama about the early years of the AIDS crisis burns with undiminished urgency in this superb Broadway revival, directed with searing intensity by Joel Grey and George C. Wolfe.
Joe Mantello's production of Larry Kramer's AIDS-era drama is a powerhouse revival that crackles with righteous anger and deep humanity.

When Larry Kramer’s "The Normal Heart" premiered off-Broadway in 1985, it had a "right here, right now" impact. Set in 1981-84 New York, it imparted a powerful, radical immediacy to almost-current events — the early years of AIDS and the burgeoning fight against that new epidemic.
"The Normal Heart" was never meant to be a subtle work.
Better than I expected, but not as well as I'd hoped.
Here is unflinching theater that is not afraid to be passionate, bold and raw.
Finally where it belongs, on Broadway, it can be seen now for the towering American tragedy that it is, as essential to our culture as "Long Day's Journey Into Night" or "Death of a Salesman."
Run to the Golden Theatre if you want to be reminded of how alive you are.
Twenty-five years since it premiered at the Public Theater, it remains a powerful example of political theater at its most direct, passionate and urgent levels.
In a Broadway season robust with bravura performances, comes another that makes demands of our souls along with our ears.
This is not a great play, to be honest.

A semi-fictionalized account of the beginning of the AIDS crisis and the efforts of a group of dedicated activists to spur the city and country into action, this work, first seen in 1985 in a landmark production at the Public Theater, is relentlessly gripping and moving.
By that point, the film’s structural and stylistic flaws hardly matter; the story’s raw emotional power has taken over.

cn.t: Kramer's searing AIDS drama retains its raw power and urgency 25+ years later, with critics praising the passionate performances and emotional impact, though some note its agitprop style can feel heavy-handed.

sg.ra: 805-seat intimate Shubert house; center Orchestra D-F is the consensus best pick across Headout, SeatPlan, and TickPick. Rows A-D play well for plays/intimate-drama given Golden's small footprint. SeatPlan notes mezzanine overhang begins at Row L with 'minimal' effect, so orchestra rear rows remain viable.
Headout and TickPick both flag center G-L as the sweet spot for value — priced below front orchestra but still before the Row L overhang line. In an 805-seat house these rows feel close regardless.

Front Mezz rows A-C center are the #2 premium pick after center orchestra — elevation gives a clean overhead line on the small Golden stage. SeatPlan flags a safety bar that can distract Row A slightly, and legroom is noted as 'slightly cramped for taller patrons.'

SeatPlan calls rear mezz 'surprisingly good' because the 805-seat footprint keeps even back rows close. Rake is described as well-designed with good elevation over Front Mezz. Legroom is the main knock — 'cramped' with narrow pitch.
